I haven't used Ubuntu in a while but I've used it for quite a few years to remember a lot of stuff. Unless you ordered a pre-packaged software with Ubuntu with some basic programs, what you're starting with will be entirely bare-bones. No browser, no software center, nothing that the average user would really use (unless something changed with newer versions of Ubuntu)

Most, if not all of your programs will primarily have to be installed via terminal commands or the Ubuntu Software Center. If this is the first time using a command line, or you're uncomfortable with it, get comfortable. You're inevitably going to be using it a lot, and that's a price that comes with using a Linux OS.

Ctrl + Alt + T to open terminal, and just copy + paste these lines to get you started:

Use this to refresh a bunch of update lists before installing anything

sudo apt-get update

Installing a central software center is nice (unless it already comes with it. mines didn't)

sudo apt-get install software-center

Use this to install Chromium

sudo apt-get install chromium-browser

Or maybe you're a Firefox guy

sudo apt-get install firefox

(At this point you have some basic browsers and can manually download packages from the internet)

btw, if you're trying something by yourself with the terminal and you're not sure if it'll mess up your system, it probably will. Always do research before messing with something.

Linux OS's are generally MUCH harder to use than other systems, but it's also that much more productive and customizable once you know how to do it.

askubuntu.com is your best friend.

Have fun using Ubuntu!

Linux has parts that are similar to Windows and parts that are dramatically different. Ubuntu is a decent choice for a beginner distro, although you might want to try one of the other flavors of it if Gnome 3 isn't your think (I am fond of Ubuntu MATE, personally, which is closer to the Linux experience). I would also recommend that you look on a search engine for this sort of question; while there are some good ideas listed on here, there are far too many things that we could list than would easily be recalled.

If anything, I just want you to know that things are going to be different (albeit quite possibly in a way you consider an improvement!) and to take some time to get used to it. Unless all you want to do us browse the web and use LibreOffice, you're probably going to have to do some learning, but it sounds like you're off to a good start by just asking.

...oh yeah, don't do anything with anything in /dev, for any reason, unless you know precisely what you're doing, why you're doing it, and what the potential side ramifications are. Be sure to verify anything you're doing there with two web sites or flat-out ask about it before you do it. And don't run 'rm -rf /', for any reason. Plus, avoid running as root, or using the 'su' or 'sudo' commands, unless you have a specific reason to, though Ubuntu gets you about 90% of the way there without even trying.

  • Image backups of your system when it's working. That way if you break something you always have an "undo" button.
  • If you delete a file off a flash drive, it's not actually deleted. Linux put it in a hidden ".trash" folder. Windows will see that folder by default.
  • Don't bother dual-booting Windows and Linux, just learn how to virtualize a Windows machine. VirtualBox is powerful and easy to use.
  • Ctrl-Alt-F2 through Ctrl-Alt-F7 takes you to command-line terminals. Ctrl-Alt-F1 takes you back to the desktop. Very handy!
  • Learn how to write scripts in BASH if you don't do programming already. Setting up some cron scripts can make your laptop very smart.
